title: Errors Are Hard To Correct
excerpt: Errors are hard to correct when users can detect that something is wrong but cannot efficiently localise, reverse, confirm, or reconstruct the correct state. The failure concerns inadequate correction support even where some recovery structure nominally exists.
metaDescription: A failure pattern where error correction is slowed by weak localisation, missing undo, side effects, uncertain confirmation, or hidden prior state.
summary: This failure describes situations where a detected error becomes difficult to correct because the interface does not support localisation, reversal, confirmation, or reconstruction of the intended state. It is distinct from failures where errors are hard to notice or where recovery paths are absent.
definition: Errors are hard to correct when a user has detected an error but the interface does not adequately support finding where it occurred, knowing the correct state, taking corrective action, or confirming that correction succeeded.
keyFacts: Error correction can fail at localisation, correct-state identification, correction action, or confirmation.
This failure concerns correction after detection, not initial error detection.
It differs from weak recovery paths because some correction structure may exist, but it is inadequate for the user's corrective attempt.
Common causes include error localisation failure, lack of an explicit undo path, correction side effects, uncertain correction confirmation, and hidden prior state.
In Gexcon CFD simulation work, corrective load fell from approximately 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes after redesign, with localisation support described as the dominant mechanism.
In shift-based operations, recovery paths must carry their own explanation because the person resolving an error may not be the person who created it.
In the Oceaneering dispatch panel case, wrong-cart-type recovery was designed so the next person in the depot could resolve the state from the panel without walking to a vehicle and resetting it.
In the Egma Order example, the refusal named the production problem but not the earlier parameter causing it, so correction was impossible for the optometrist without support intervention.
In visioncheckout, correction was designed as a product surface through the Corrector rather than treated as a rare error branch.
bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Errors are hard to correct when a user has detected that something is wrong but cannot efficiently return the system to the intended state. Error correction depends on several components: localising where the error occurred, understanding what the state should be instead, taking the correction action, and confirming that the correction succeeded.

This failure is not the same as an absent recovery path. It describes situations where correction structures nominally exist, but the interface does not support the user's corrective attempt well enough. The user is trying to correct the error; the interface makes that correction longer, more effortful, or more error-prone than the original error warranted.

## Failure pattern: correction fails after detection

Errors are hard to correct after detection when the interface does not help the user answer four operational questions: where the error happened, what the correct state should be, how to change the incorrect state, and whether the change worked.

The failure often appears after a warning, refusal, alarm, interrupted sequence, invalid configuration, or mistaken selection. The interface may communicate that something is wrong without communicating the location, cause, scope, or expected correction. In those conditions, the user must search, infer, reconstruct, or repeat work before a targeted correction is possible.

The correction process can become larger than the original error. A small parameter error can require searching many configuration values. A refused order can become a support ticket. A wrong-cart-type state can require a physical trip if the panel does not carry the required explanation. A correction can also create new errors if the corrective action changes related fields, rules, or outputs.

## Distinction from hard-to-notice errors and weak recovery paths

Errors are hard to correct is sequentially related to errors are hard to notice, but the two failures describe different stages. Errors are hard to notice concerns detection. Errors are hard to correct concerns the correction process after detection. A delayed detection can make correction harder because the error has had time to propagate, but the correction failure is still the lack of support once the user is trying to fix the state.

Errors are hard to correct is also distinct from weak recovery paths. Weak recovery paths concern the structural absence of recovery support. Errors are hard to correct concerns correction difficulty when a recovery structure or correction route exists in some form but does not provide enough localisation, prior state, scope, action clarity, or confirmation.

## What causes errors to be hard to correct

Error localisation failure occurs when the user knows an error has happened but cannot determine where in the workflow, configuration, or dataset it occurred. Correction requires knowing what to fix. Without localisation, the user must search the whole system or guess.

Missing undo paths make correction difficult when the system has no direct reversal mechanism for the error category. The user cannot undo the action and must reconstruct the correct state manually from the current incorrect state. In complex configurations, this can require understanding the dependency chain around the error.

Correction-side-effect errors occur when the corrective action changes other elements the user did not intend to change. Correcting one field can change dependent fields. Correcting one policy rule can alter its interaction with other rules. Correcting one parameter can change outputs that had already been verified. Correction then creates new correction work.

Uncertain correction confirmation occurs when the user cannot tell whether the correction succeeded. The system has changed, but the interface does not confirm whether the intended state was reached. The user either investigates again, adding overhead, or accepts uncertainty, increasing the risk that a remaining error will propagate.

Hidden prior state makes correction difficult when the correct state depends on knowing what existed before the error. If the interface does not show the previous value, prior configuration, or interrupted sequence state, the user must reconstruct it from memory or external records.

## Recovery across handover requires the correction path to explain itself

Errors are hard to correct in shift-based operations when the person resolving an error is not the person who created it. Recovery designed around a single continuous user assumes continuity of attention that the operation may not provide. The next person into the area inherits a state they did not create and may not be able to interpret.

In these conditions, the recovery path must carry its own explanation. The interface needs to state what the system detected, what had been requested, and what action is needed. Relying on the memory of the person who acted is insufficient when the error is detected after that person has left.

## How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses correction difficulty

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses correction difficulty by treating correction as an explicit interaction sequence, not as a secondary error branch. In the documented examples, the design response depends on which part of correction fails: localisation, reversal, side effects, confirmation, prior state visibility, or handover context.

When localisation is the dominant cost, correction support needs to show what is wrong and where it is located. In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, the correction action itself was fast; the expensive part was finding the configuration value responsible for the detected error.

When correction is reversible, a direct undo path can reduce reconstruction work. In the Assemblio case, Assemblio described a product with no undo. The designed response offered undo in the snack bar for reversible actions such as move and rename, with the engagement record marking the feature as client-requested and unconfirmed at item level.

When correction can invalidate later work, the interface needs to warn about the correction cost before the change is committed. In the Egma Order case, cascade invalidation was designed so that editing a completed earlier section warns the user that subsequent sections will be emptied and offers apply-change or discard.

When correction is structurally impossible, prevention becomes the correction strategy. In the Dancerace / Jacko example, irreversible financial actions were handled with proportional confirmation friction before the action rather than undo afterwards.

## Evidence basis from documented cases

### Gexcon CFD simulation shows localisation as the dominant correction cost

In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, a detected configuration error previously required identifying which of many configuration parameters was responsible, understanding the intended value, making the change, and re-running the simulation. Available case evidence records that, without support for localisation, finding the relevant parameter consumed most of a 4–6 hour corrective load.

After the redesign, corrective load fell to approximately 20 minutes, measured by Gexcon across real deployments. The documented mechanism was localisation support: the redesigned error communication specified what was wrong and where in the configuration. The case distinguishes the diagnostic burden from the correction action itself, because changing a configuration value was already fast once the correct value was found.

### Kardion MCS Controller shows correction as a completed alarm sequence

In the Kardion MCS Controller case, alarm acknowledgement required a correction sequence: perceive the alarm, understand its meaning, take the appropriate clinical action, acknowledge the alarm, and confirm that the condition had resolved.

The correction sequence could remain incomplete if an alarm was muted but not acknowledged, or acknowledged without confirmation that the condition had resolved. Muted alarms remaining visible was the interface mechanism that prevented incomplete correction sequences from becoming invisible. The case shows that acknowledgement alone is not equivalent to correction confirmation.

### Beissbarth automotive calibration shows prior state and correction scope after interruption

In the Beissbarth automotive calibration case, an interrupted calibration sequence required the technician to resume from the correct point. Resumption depended on knowing which steps had been completed and verified, which step failed and why, and which steps needed to be repeated.

A sequence state display that showed only the current step did not provide enough information to assess correction scope. Without completed and upcoming steps, technicians could redo steps that had already been completed correctly or skip steps that needed repetition.

### Oceaneering dispatch panel shows handover recovery without a physical reset trip

In the Oceaneering dispatch panel case, the subject was a wall-mounted touchscreen in a logistics depot through which a materials-handling operator puts a cart into an automated hospital transport system. In the system being replaced, recovery from a wrong-cart-type error required staff to walk to the vehicle and reset it so it would leave; it could not be done from the panel.

The designed wrong-cart-type recovery allowed the station holding the refused cart to be tapped on the panel. The panel presented what the vehicle detected against what was selected, allowed the detected type to be confirmed in one action, and allowed the destination and identity to be re-entered. This design addressed the handover condition by giving the next person in the depot enough information to resolve the state without walking to the vehicle.

The available evidence for this case has defined limits. The before state came from the predecessor's own specification and from interviews with people adjacent to the users. No dispatch operator was interviewed, no depot was visited, and the design was reviewed with operations managers. No task was attempted and nothing was measured.

### Assemblio shows undo for reversible actions where no undo existed

In the Assemblio case, Assemblio described the Assemblio Composer and Smart Viewer as having no undo. The design response offered undo in the snack bar for reversible actions such as move and rename.

The available evidence is limited to Assemblio's account of its own product and the engagement record. The product description is client-stated, not observed. The snack-bar undo feature is recorded as client-requested, with an item-level marker that is unconfirmed.

### Egma Order shows a refusal that named the problem but not the cause

In the Egma Order case, the support team's worked example described an optometrist trying to order a pair of reading lenses and reaching a refusal after completing about half the steps. The refusal said: "Lenses with your selected shape cannot be produced. Please choose a different shape."

The correction problem was localisation. The patient did not want a different lens shape, and the optometrist could not determine which of a dozen earlier parameters needed to change to allow the intended shape. The result was a support ticket instead of an order, and the support team placed the order on the optometrist's behalf.

The designed answer was cascade invalidation warned before it happens. When a user edits a completed earlier section, the interface states before the change is committed that all subsequent sections will be emptied, and offers apply-change or discard. The platform is live, but no support-ticket movement, order-completion rate, or other outcome was measured.

### visioncheckout treats correction as a product surface

In the visioncheckout case, visioncheckout is a German vendor of computer-vision self-checkout systems for staff restaurants and catering. The product was in development and nothing had shipped.

The Corrector made correction a designed product surface rather than a hidden branch. Numbered markers on the tray image were matched to a numbered list. Thumbnails were required in the catalogue because item names were often not meaningful enough to identify a dish without an image. Sidebar category navigation was chosen, and search was deliberately de-emphasised so scrolling thumbnails remained the primary path, with search still available for staff.

Several correction decisions were explicitly bounded. Scrolling was preferred over pagination because the touchscreen was responsive enough. Auto-cycling variant thumbnails were ruled out on accessibility grounds and as visual noise, leaving the one-POS-item-to-many-visual-variants problem unresolved rather than hidden. Entry to the Corrector was deliberately understated through a tertiary edit control near the basket header, with rescan remaining the primary action.

The rescan action was flagged as destructive because it discarded all state, including corrections already made, with a two-step confirmation recommended wherever corrections exist. The governing interaction principle for Selections, Extras, and the Corrector was to present the interaction as "confirm this", not as "fix this". Published recognition-accuracy claims in this product category are vendor-reported, methodologically heterogeneous, and rarely independently replicated; the documented case gives no accuracy number for any named product. Published self-checkout operations research finds roughly one help call to staff per ten self-checkout transactions, supporting the framing of intervention as routine load rather than an edge case.

## Boundaries and limits

This failure page does not claim that every documented design response produced a measured outcome. The Gexcon corrective-load reduction is measured by Gexcon across real deployments. Several other examples document design decisions, reported problems, or reviewed designs without measured post-launch effects.

The Oceaneering case records no efficiency, error-rate, or dispatch-volume outcome. The work concerned hospital logistics infrastructure, not medical-device work. The design was reviewed with operations managers, no dispatch operator took part, no task was attempted, and nothing was measured.

The Assemblio product description is client-stated and not observed. No time-saving, error-rate, adoption, or marketing outcome is established for Assemblio.

The Egma Order platform is live, but no support-ticket movement, order-completion rate, or other outcome was measured. The documented evidence establishes the correction problem and design response, not a post-launch result.

The visioncheckout product was in development, nothing had shipped, and no throughput, speed, error-rate, or recognition-accuracy outcome is established for the redesign. No competitor recognition-accuracy number should be treated as measured truth from this case.

## Related pages

This failure is closely related to errors that are hard to notice because undetected errors can propagate before correction begins. It is also related to weak recovery paths, because inadequate correction support can resemble absent recovery support when the user has no practical way to restore the intended state.

Errors are hard to correct also overlaps with failures where users cannot confirm that an action worked, where the interface does not make clear what an action will affect, and where handoffs lose context. These related failures describe narrower mechanisms that can make correction longer, riskier, or dependent on memory outside the interface.
